=== MULTI-SOURCE TOPIC CLUSTER: At Gresham’s ‘No Kings’ protest, Latinos push to get out the vote ===

[Source 1 — www.opb.org] (URL: https://www.opb.org/article/2026/10/17/at-greshams-no-kings-protest-latinos-push-to-get-out-the-vote/):
Stated Claim / Post Context:
At Gresham’s ‘No Kings’ protest, Latinos push to get out the vote

After an uptick in immigration arrests, Latino organizers encourage fearful community members to still turn in their ballots for a high-stakes midterm election

Actual Article Body:
Independent. Member-supported.For the Pacific Northwest.

Independent.Member-supported.

A voter drops off her ballot at the East County Library during the fourth iteration of “No Kings” protests in Gresham, Ore., on Oct. 17, 2026.

Jireh Deng / OPB

Protesters across Oregon rallied Saturday for the fourth iteration of the “No Kings” protest since President Donald Trump returned to office. The focus was to get out the vote.

In Oregon’s fourth-most populous city, Gresham, Latino civic leaders spoke to constituents, particularly addressing fears of voter intimidation at the polls. The week prior, OPB reported a jump in immigration arrests in East Multnomah County. About one in five residents in Gresham identify as Hispanic.

¡Sí se puede! ¡Sí se puede!” said State Rep. Ricki Ruiz, D-Gresham, as he led a crowd of over 300 people in a chant outside Gresham City Hall. People brought colorful hand-drawn signs with anti-Trump and anti-Elon Musk slogans while sporting pins that stated, “I voted.”

Clave 503, a local Mexican-American band, plays while walking with a contingent of Latino voters towards Gresham City Hall during the fourth “No Kings” protest in Gresham, Ore., on Oct. 17, 2026.

Jireh Deng / OPB

Multnomah County Chair Jessica Vega Pederson shared her pride at being the first Latina elected to her position, telling the rally that her grandfather immigrated to the United States from Mexico to realize his American dream. “There is so much fear because of the intimidation that is happening,” Vega Pederson said of ICE’s aggressive tactics in profiling and arresting people.

She hopes that by speaking out about her identity and family’s immigration story, residents will see themselves reflected in her experiences. “I want people in the community to understand that folks are welcome here.”

A handful of counterprotesters, one wearing a sweater that read “King Trump,” carried selfie sticks as they chanted “God Bless Donald Trump” and “God Bless ICE.” But neither the heated confrontations nor the rainy weather deterred the festivities of the Latino cohort that had gathered at Gresham City Hall.

First image:  Alicia Arana, a volunteer with Multnomah East Indivisible, holds up ballots while wearing a red tulle wig at the rally. Second image:  A protester wears a Trump mask in an orange prison jumpsuit costume.

All images: Jireh Deng / OPB.

The main contingent of “No Kings” demonstrators marched into the intersection of Eastman Parkway and Division Street to raise their protest signage as a group of Latina joggers finished a 5K run to the cheers of onlookers and live music by a Portland-based Mexican band.

“More than ever our community is feeling unsafe being out and about,” said Saray Garcia, a Gresham resident who is part of the running crew, Latinas Run Across Portland.

Garcia said running together carries safety in numbers as women of color take up space together. On the running club’s pink T-shirts was the phrase in Spanish, “juntas somos más fuertes,” or “together we are stronger.” At least two people Garcia knew stopped coming to the running meetups because of recent ICE activity in the Portland metro area, she told OPB.

“We’re representing our culture, and we’re showing up for the community that’s not able to vote,” she said. Garcia and others celebrated the end of the 5K by dropping off their mail-in ballots at the nearby East County Library. “We want to be the voice for them.”

Saray Garcia, center, stands with members of her run club, Latinas Run Across Portland, as they cheer on joggers who finished their five-kilometer run.

Jireh Deng / OPB

Ruiz’s office had organized the performance by the band Clave 503 as well as the vendor Sabor Valdex, who served up infused Red Bulls and bagels with cream cheese. Heavy on Ruiz’s mind was the recent school shooting in Bend, where three children and a teacher had been killed. To him, it felt all the more important to get out the vote in this upcoming midterm to create change.

“A lot of these things that we’ve seen happening across the state and across this nation are policy decisions that are made at the congressional level,” Ruiz said. “We do our best to respond with action, and I think part of that is turning out to vote.”

U.S. Rep. Maxine Dexter, D-Portland, who is up for reelection, also spoke at the protest, encouraging people to make sure their voices were heard through their votes.

She told OPB that she visited Portland’s ICE detention center with her colleagues Sen. Jeff Merkley and Rep. Suzanne Bonamici last week, trying to track down one of her constituents who was arrested.

U.S. House Rep. Maxine Dexter addresses protestors, encouraging them to vote in the upcoming midterm elections.

Jireh Deng / OPB

“They’re going straight to Tacoma,” she said of detainees picked up in the Portland metro area. She called it a denial of due process.

“People are feeling targeted,” Dexter said. “The worst part of this, though, is that people are afraid to reach out to the government right now.”

Dexter said she was committed to challenging the Trump administration’s immigration campaigns and to visiting immigration detention facilities to oversee them as her right as a member of Congress.

Election Day is Tuesday, Nov. 3. Stay informed with OPB on the Oregon governor's race and other regional contests in Oregon and Southwest Washington at our ballot guide.

‘No Kings’ protesters spurn organizers' rules: ‘This is as partisan as you can get’

Protesters at official No Kings events openly urged voters to "vote blue" and elect Democrats, directly contradicting organizers' nonpartisan rules.

Actual Article Body:
This material may not be published, broadcast, rewritten, or redistributed. ©2026 FOX News Network, LLC. All rights reserved. Quotes displayed in real-time or delayed by at least 15 minutes. Market data provided by Factset. Powered and implemented by FactSet Digital Solutions. Legal Statement. Mutual Fund and ETF data provided by LSEG.

At an official

ALEXANDRIA, Va. — On South Washington Street, 26-year-old environmental engineer Nayely Cruz Hernandez had a straightforward message for voters as she joined a phalanx of protesters lining the street for nationwide "No Kings" protests against President Donald Trump: "Vote blue."

"We got to take the power away from Trump, from the Republicans," Hernandez told Fox News Digital. "So we got to win the House, we got to win the Senate, not only in Virginia, but across the country."

Standing beside her boyfriend, Noah Schwarzott, 25, their 13-year-old Maltese-poodle, Maybellene, in her arms, Hernandez acknowledged that national No Kings organizers had their own rules for the protests to be "nonpartisan," but she wasn't following orders.

'NO KINGS' FOOT SOLDIERS IGNORE ORGANIZERS' WARNING, GO ALL IN FOR DEMOCRATS

Demonstrators rally in Alexandria, Va, as part of the nationwide "No Kings" protest on Oct. 17, 2026. (Asra Q. Nomani/Fox News Digital)

"The No King ... organizers can say whatever," she said. "But I'm saying vote blue, because why are we here? Who's in the House? Who's in the Senate? Who is the President? It's red, it's Republicans, and it's Trump."

A Fox News Digital investigation documented about 300 organizations with $2.5 billion in combined annual revenues behind the "No Kings" protest network, including Democratic-aligned advocacy groups, major labor unions and nonprofits including MoveOn, the American Federation of Teachers and the ACLU.

Cruz Hernandez ended by introducing Maybellene and declaring that the dog was "telling you to vote for Don Beyer," a Democratic member of Congress who represents Alexandria, Arlington and other Northern Virginia communities.

The national organizers' position is that the Oct. 17 events must be "nonpartisan." That's to comply with the federal laws that regulate the nonprofits that fund the No Kings protests.

Crowds gather in Alexandria, Va., for the "No Kings" protest. (Asra Q. Nomani/Fox News Digital)

PARTY POOPERS' FIGHT CARD: JANE FONDA, 'NO KINGS,' COMMUNISTS ROLL OUT RIVAL SPECTACLE TO TRUMP'S 250TH

Her comments directly contradicted the written instructions of the national "No Kings" organization and its leaders at the Indivisible nonprofit, prohibiting calls to "vote Blue," elect Democrats or endorse candidates and target individuals.

Nearby, a man held a sign by a far-left group called "Refuse Fascism" with another message defying the organizers' guidance: "TRUMP MUST GO NOW!" Another man held an inflatable balloon mocking Trump as a baby in a diaper. Another sign said "86 47," the controversial message former FBI Director James Comey posted on social media and which federal prosecutors deemed an overt threat against Trump.

As the young couple cheered honking cars, Eunic Epstein-Ortiz, national spokesperson for No Kings, called Fox News Digital to insist "No Kings" is a "nonpartisan, peaceful movement that has brought millions of Americans together to stand up for democracy, defend our freedoms, and reject authoritarianism."

DAVID MARCUS: AS DEMOCRATS PROTEST IN DALLAS, CONSERVATIVES ARE QUIET AND CAUTIOUS

Told that a Fox News DIgital investigation found "No Kings" events from Maine to Oregon were clearly partisan, Epstein-Ortiz said, "We are aware of partisan events circulating online that are not affiliated with or officially organized by No Kings. Many people utilize the No Kings name as a rallying cry."

But, in this case, the protest on South Washington Street was an official "No Kings" event, advertised on the organizers' official website.

"No Kings" organizers provide a list of "Do" and "Don't warnings for their Oct. 17, 2025, voter event. (No Kings)

Among the demonstrators, one woman beamed while waving a sign that was explicit about the protest's agenda: "THE USA Needs a Big Beautiful BLUE WAVE."

But hours after the Alexandria demonstration, Fox News Digital encountered another protester marching on H Street NW by the White House who openly rejected the nonpartisan description. She marched at an official "No Kings" event.

Nadine Seiler, a self-described "professional protester" recently mentioned by Trump, was asked whether she agreed with organizers' insistence that the demonstration was nonpartisan.

"No, no, the people who agree with Trump are not out here," Seiler responded from behind an inflatable costume. "So it's never gonna be non-partisan if it's a resistance to the fascist regime."

"They can pretend, but it's not," she added.

"No Kings" organizers provide a list of "Event Prohibitions" for their Oct. 17, 2025, voter event. (No Kings)

Asked directly whether the event was partisan, Seiler answered: "Yes, this is a partisan protest."

She explained that participants were resisting what she described as illegal policies of the Trump administration.

"Yeah, so this is as partisan as you can get," she concluded.

The exchanges offer a ground-level perspective on the political character of a movement whose organizers have gone to considerable lengths to insist its voter-mobilization activities are "nonpartisan."

A crowd participates in the "No Kings" rally in Alexandria, Va. (Asra Q. Nomani/Fox News Digital)

FIRST ON FOX: ‘NO KINGS’ PROTEST NETWORK BEHIND FIGHT AGAINST AI DATA CENTERS AND FLOCK CAMERAS

"No Kings" has distributed detailed election-law guidance prohibiting partisan slogans, campaign materials, candidate endorsements and coordination with political parties.

Yet the movement's own leadership has openly discussed its broader Democratic electoral objectives.

During an Oct. 15 livestream, Indivisible co-founder Ezra Levin contrasted the parties' candidates.

Protesters hold signs during the "No Kings" demonstration in Alexandria, Va. (Asra Q. Nomani/Fox News Digital)

"Our candidates are quite good all around the country. Their candidates are quite trash all over the country," Levin said.

In an Oct. 9 webinar, Levin explained how activists could criticize Trump while avoiding explicit Democratic endorsements.

"Uh, you've got to let people connect the dots on that one," he said.

Indivisible co-founder Leah Greenberg, meanwhile, described No Kings as a "nonpartisan coalition" intended to welcome participants across the political spectrum.

Demonstrators rally in Alexandria, Va., as part of the nationwide "No Kings" protest. (Asra Q. Nomani/Fox News Digital)

The distinction matters legally. Individual protesters expressing partisan opinions don't automatically establish that event organizers violated election law. Tax-exempt charities also face restrictions different from those governing political advocacy groups. In yet another sign, a protester again targeted Trump, writing, "EVERY DAY I HATE HIM MORE THAN I DID THE DAY BEFORE." Another sign read: "NO CROWN FOR THE CLOWN."

From northern Virginia to the White House, participants were making no effort to conceal their political preferences.

For Seiler, the description was simple: "This is as partisan as you can get."

Fox News Digital's Reagan Schroeder and Tessa Hoyos contributed to this report.

Asra Nomani is senior editor of investigations at Fox News Digital. She is a former reporter at the Wall Street Journal, where she covered stories related to money, politics and society. She is the author of "Woke Army: The Red-Green Alliance That Is Undermining America’s Freedom." She can be reached at asra.nomani@fox.com and on X at @asranomani.

Two people in custody after protest at offshore Woodside gas platform

Two people are in police custody after occupying an offshore Woodside platform about 200 kilometres off Western Australia's coast to protest against the company's gas operations.

By Cason Ho

Topic:Oil and Gas

Greenpeace say activists spent the night on the platform.  (Supplied: Greenpeace)

Two people are in police custody after occupying an offshore Woodside gas platform about 200 kilometres off Western Australia's coast to protest against the company's gas operations.

An Australian Border Force (ABF) spokesperson said they were working with federal and state agencies to respond to the situation after activists occupied the rig overnight and disrupted the gas giant's operations.

Images shared by environmental advocacy group Greenpeace Australia Pacific show its activists scaling a Woodside gas platform and hanging a banner in protest of the company's planned gas project at Scott Reef.

Greenpeace said four protesters travelled to the platform early Saturday morning, and two of them set up "temporary hanging tents" to occupy the platform for "as long as possible".

On Sunday afternoon Greenpeace said two of its activists had been taken into police custody.

Protesters scaled a gas platform operated by Woodside. (Supplied: Greenpeace)

"Special police forces landed a helicopter on the [platform] at around 11:30am AWST," Greenpeace said.

"The activists safely removed themselves from their equipment before being taken into police custody around 1pm."

Woodside confirmed the protest had disrupted operations at the rig, which forms part of the company's $12.5 billion Scarborough natural gas project.

"Pre-commissioning activities at Scarborough have been paused as part of routine procedures following the unauthorised access," a spokesperson said.

Scott Reef is Australia's largest standalone oceanic reef and a refuge for thousands of aquatic creatures and shorebirds — Woodside's plans have been heavily contested by environmental groups opposed to gas developments in the area.

Woodside's Browse gas project plans to tap into Australia's largest undeveloped offshore gas reserve, and is estimated to cost about $48.7 billion according to a Deloitte analysis.

A banner unfurled by protesters at a Woodside gas platform.  (Supplied: Greenpeace)

Woodside said Greenpeace's activists had "deliberately and unlawfully" accessed the floating production unit and had "not only endangered their own safety, but that of Woodside staff".

"Greenpeace's actions have triggered a significant, potentially costly and entirely avoidable response, requiring Western Australian resources to be mobilised to manage the safety, security and operational consequences of their actions," a Woodside spokesperson said.

Greenpeace Australia Pacific CEO David Ritter said the activists involved in the latest demonstration were "highly trained and experienced", and said care was "always taken in the health, safety and welfare of all involved".

He said environmental groups had been scaling up their activism in response to Woodside's planned Browse project.

"Greenpeace and other community organisations have been building up their activities matching that rise in community concern," Mr Ritter told the ABC.

"There is no question that our activities are increasing to match this reckless threat of Woodside."

She hopes that by speaking out about her identity and family’s immigration story, residents will see themselves reflected in her experiences. “I want people in the community to understand that folks are welcome here.”

A handful of counterprotesters, one wearing a sweater that read “King Trump,” carried selfie sticks as they chanted “God Bless Donald Trump” and “God Bless ICE.” But neither the heated confrontations nor the rainy weather deterred the festivities of the Latino cohort that had gathered at Gresham City Hall.

First image:  Alicia Arana, a volunteer with Multnomah East Indivisible, holds up ballots while wearing a red tulle wig at the rally. Second image:  A protester wears a Trump mask in an orange prison jumpsuit costume.

All images: Jireh Deng / OPB.

The main contingent of “No Kings” demonstrators marched into the intersection of Eastman Parkway and Division Street to raise their protest signage as a group of Latina joggers finished a 5K run to the cheers of onlookers and live music by a Portland-based Mexican band.

“More than ever our community is feeling unsafe being out and about,” said Saray Garcia, a Gresham resident who is part of the running crew, Latinas Run Across Portland.

Garcia said running together carries safety in numbers as women of color take up space together. On the running club’s pink T-shirts was the phrase in Spanish, “juntas somos más fuertes,” or “together we are stronger.” At least two people Garcia knew stopped coming to the running meetups because of recent ICE activity in the Portland metro area, she told OPB.

“We’re representing our culture, and we’re showing up for the community that’s not able to vote,” she said. Garcia and others celebrated the end of the 5K by dropping off their mail-in ballots at the nearby East County Library. “We want to be the voice for them.”

Saray Garcia, center, stands with members of her run club, Latinas Run Across Portland, as they cheer on joggers who finished their five-kilometer run.

Jireh Deng / OPB

Ruiz’s office had organized the performance by the band Clave 503 as well as the vendor Sabor Valdex, who served up infused Red Bulls and bagels with cream cheese. Heavy on Ruiz’s mind was the recent school shooting in Bend, where three children and a teacher had been killed. To him, it felt all the more important to get out the vote in this upcoming midterm to create change.

“A lot of these things that we’ve seen happening across the state and across this nation are policy decisions that are made at the congressional level,” Ruiz said. “We do our best to respond with action, and I think part of that is turning out to vote.”

U.S. Rep. Maxine Dexter, D-Portland, who is up for reelection, also spoke at the protest, encouraging people to make sure their voices were heard through their votes.

She told OPB that she visited Portland’s ICE detention center with her colleagues Sen. Jeff Merkley and Rep. Suzanne Bonamici last week, trying to track down one of her constituents who was arrested.

U.S. House Rep. Maxine Dexter addresses protestors, encouraging them to vote in the upcoming midterm elections.

Jireh Deng / OPB

“They’re going straight to Tacoma,” she said of detainees picked up in the Portland metro area. She called it a denial of due process.

“People are feeling targeted,” Dexter said. “The worst part of this, though, is that people are afraid to reach out to the government right now.”

Dexter said she was committed to challenging the Trump administration’s immigration campaigns and to visiting immigration detention facilities to oversee them as her right as a member of Congress.

‘No Kings’ protesters spurn organizers' rules: ‘This is as partisan as you can get’

Protesters at official No Kings events openly urged voters to "vote blue" and elect Democrats, directly contradicting organizers' nonpartisan rules.

At an official

ALEXANDRIA, Va. — On South Washington Street, 26-year-old environmental engineer Nayely Cruz Hernandez had a straightforward message for voters as she joined a phalanx of protesters lining the street for nationwide "No Kings" protests against President Donald Trump: "Vote blue."

"We got to take the power away from Trump, from the Republicans," Hernandez told Fox News Digital. "So we got to win the House, we got to win the Senate, not only in Virginia, but across the country."

Standing beside her boyfriend, Noah Schwarzott, 25, their 13-year-old Maltese-poodle, Maybellene, in her arms, Hernandez acknowledged that national No Kings organizers had their own rules for the protests to be "nonpartisan," but she wasn't following orders.

'NO KINGS' FOOT SOLDIERS IGNORE ORGANIZERS' WARNING, GO ALL IN FOR DEMOCRATS

Demonstrators rally in Alexandria, Va, as part of the nationwide "No Kings" protest on Oct. 17, 2026. (Asra Q. Nomani/Fox News Digital)

"The No King ... organizers can say whatever," she said. "But I'm saying vote blue, because why are we here? Who's in the House? Who's in the Senate? Who is the President? It's red, it's Republicans, and it's Trump."

A Fox News Digital investigation documented about 300 organizations with $2.5 billion in combined annual revenues behind the "No Kings" protest network, including Democratic-aligned advocacy groups, major labor unions and nonprofits including MoveOn, the American Federation of Teachers and the ACLU.

Cruz Hernandez ended by introducing Maybellene and declaring that the dog was "telling you to vote for Don Beyer," a Democratic member of Congress who represents Alexandria, Arlington and other Northern Virginia communities.

The national organizers' position is that the Oct. 17 events must be "nonpartisan." That's to comply with the federal laws that regulate the nonprofits that fund the No Kings protests.

Crowds gather in Alexandria, Va., for the "No Kings" protest. (Asra Q. Nomani/Fox News Digital)

PARTY POOPERS' FIGHT CARD: JANE FONDA, 'NO KINGS,' COMMUNISTS ROLL OUT RIVAL SPECTACLE TO TRUMP'S 250TH

Her comments directly contradicted the written instructions of the national "No Kings" organization and its leaders at the Indivisible nonprofit, prohibiting calls to "vote Blue," elect Democrats or endorse candidates and target individuals.

Nearby, a man held a sign by a far-left group called "Refuse Fascism" with another message defying the organizers' guidance: "TRUMP MUST GO NOW!" Another man held an inflatable balloon mocking Trump as a baby in a diaper. Another sign said "86 47," the controversial message former FBI Director James Comey posted on social media and which federal prosecutors deemed an overt threat against Trump.

As the young couple cheered honking cars, Eunic Epstein-Ortiz, national spokesperson for No Kings, called Fox News Digital to insist "No Kings" is a "nonpartisan, peaceful movement that has brought millions of Americans together to stand up for democracy, defend our freedoms, and reject authoritarianism."

DAVID MARCUS: AS DEMOCRATS PROTEST IN DALLAS, CONSERVATIVES ARE QUIET AND CAUTIOUS

Told that a Fox News DIgital investigation found "No Kings" events from Maine to Oregon were clearly partisan, Epstein-Ortiz said, "We are aware of partisan events circulating online that are not affiliated with or officially organized by No Kings. Many people utilize the No Kings name as a rallying cry."

But, in this case, the protest on South Washington Street was an official "No Kings" event, advertised on the organizers' official website.

"No Kings" organizers provide a list of "Do" and "Don't warnings for their Oct. 17, 2025, voter event. (No Kings)

Among the demonstrators, one woman beamed while waving a sign that was explicit about the protest's agenda: "THE USA Needs a Big Beautiful BLUE WAVE."

But hours after the Alexandria demonstration, Fox News Digital encountered another protester marching on H Street NW by the White House who openly rejected the nonpartisan description. She marched at an official "No Kings" event.

Nadine Seiler, a self-described "professional protester" recently mentioned by Trump, was asked whether she agreed with organizers' insistence that the demonstration was nonpartisan.

"No, no, the people who agree with Trump are not out here," Seiler responded from behind an inflatable costume. "So it's never gonna be non-partisan if it's a resistance to the fascist regime."

"They can pretend, but it's not," she added.

"No Kings" organizers provide a list of "Event Prohibitions" for their Oct. 17, 2025, voter event. (No Kings)

Asked directly whether the event was partisan, Seiler answered: "Yes, this is a partisan protest."

She explained that participants were resisting what she described as illegal policies of the Trump administration.

"Yeah, so this is as partisan as you can get," she concluded.

The exchanges offer a ground-level perspective on the political character of a movement whose organizers have gone to considerable lengths to insist its voter-mobilization activities are "nonpartisan."

A crowd participates in the "No Kings" rally in Alexandria, Va. (Asra Q. Nomani/Fox News Digital)

FIRST ON FOX: ‘NO KINGS’ PROTEST NETWORK BEHIND FIGHT AGAINST AI DATA CENTERS AND FLOCK CAMERAS

"No Kings" has distributed detailed election-law guidance prohibiting partisan slogans, campaign materials, candidate endorsements and coordination with political parties.

Yet the movement's own leadership has openly discussed its broader Democratic electoral objectives.

During an Oct. 15 livestream, Indivisible co-founder Ezra Levin contrasted the parties' candidates.

Protesters hold signs during the "No Kings" demonstration in Alexandria, Va. (Asra Q. Nomani/Fox News Digital)

"Our candidates are quite good all around the country. Their candidates are quite trash all over the country," Levin said.

In an Oct. 9 webinar, Levin explained how activists could criticize Trump while avoiding explicit Democratic endorsements.

"Uh, you've got to let people connect the dots on that one," he said.

Indivisible co-founder Leah Greenberg, meanwhile, described No Kings as a "nonpartisan coalition" intended to welcome participants across the political spectrum.

Demonstrators rally in Alexandria, Va., as part of the nationwide "No Kings" protest. (Asra Q. Nomani/Fox News Digital)

The distinction matters legally. Individual protesters expressing partisan opinions don't automatically establish that event organizers violated election law. Tax-exempt charities also face restrictions different from those governing political advocacy groups. In yet another sign, a protester again targeted Trump, writing, "EVERY DAY I HATE HIM MORE THAN I DID THE DAY BEFORE." Another sign read: "NO CROWN FOR THE CLOWN."

From northern Virginia to the White House, participants were making no effort to conceal their political preferences.

For Seiler, the description was simple: "This is as partisan as you can get."

Two people in custody after protest at offshore Woodside gas platform

Two people are in police custody after occupying an offshore Woodside platform about 200 kilometres off Western Australia's coast to protest against the company's gas operations.

Actual Article Body:

By Cason Ho

Topic:Oil and Gas

Greenpeace say activists spent the night on the platform.  (Supplied: Greenpeace)

Two people are in police custody after occupying an offshore Woodside gas platform about 200 kilometres off Western Australia's coast to protest against the company's gas operations.

An Australian Border Force (ABF) spokesperson said they were working with federal and state agencies to respond to the situation after activists occupied the rig overnight and disrupted the gas giant's operations.

Images shared by environmental advocacy group Greenpeace Australia Pacific show its activists scaling a Woodside gas platform and hanging a banner in protest of the company's planned gas project at Scott Reef.

Greenpeace said four protesters travelled to the platform early Saturday morning, and two of them set up "temporary hanging tents" to occupy the platform for "as long as possible".

On Sunday afternoon Greenpeace said two of its activists had been taken into police custody.

Protesters scaled a gas platform operated by Woodside. (Supplied: Greenpeace)

"Special police forces landed a helicopter on the [platform] at around 11:30am AWST," Greenpeace said.

"The activists safely removed themselves from their equipment before being taken into police custody around 1pm."

Woodside confirmed the protest had disrupted operations at the rig, which forms part of the company's $12.5 billion Scarborough natural gas project.

"Pre-commissioning activities at Scarborough have been paused as part of routine procedures following the unauthorised access," a spokesperson said.

Scott Reef is Australia's largest standalone oceanic reef and a refuge for thousands of aquatic creatures and shorebirds — Woodside's plans have been heavily contested by environmental groups opposed to gas developments in the area.

Woodside's Browse gas project plans to tap into Australia's largest undeveloped offshore gas reserve, and is estimated to cost about $48.7 billion according to a Deloitte analysis.

A banner unfurled by protesters at a Woodside gas platform.  (Supplied: Greenpeace)

Woodside said Greenpeace's activists had "deliberately and unlawfully" accessed the floating production unit and had "not only endangered their own safety, but that of Woodside staff".

"Greenpeace's actions have triggered a significant, potentially costly and entirely avoidable response, requiring Western Australian resources to be mobilised to manage the safety, security and operational consequences of their actions," a Woodside spokesperson said.

Greenpeace Australia Pacific CEO David Ritter said the activists involved in the latest demonstration were "highly trained and experienced", and said care was "always taken in the health, safety and welfare of all involved".

He said environmental groups had been scaling up their activism in response to Woodside's planned Browse project.

"Greenpeace and other community organisations have been building up their activities matching that rise in community concern," Mr Ritter told the ABC.

"There is no question that our activities are increasing to match this reckless threat of Woodside."
